question: Does pretraining on solutions that make an error and immediately retry with a correction teach a language model more robust grade-school-math reasoning than the same amount of clean solution data?

key_findings.claim: On the controlled synthetic math distribution, retry trajectories improve direct autoregressive solution accuracy over token-matched clean pretraining.
key_findings.evidence: Training examples include a plausible wrong step, an explicit retry marker, and a corrected continuation. At evaluation the model is prompted normally and need not emit a retry. Across model/data settings the reported advantage persists relative to clean data and cannot be reproduced merely by beam search over a clean model.

key_findings.claim: Models trained with high retry rates rarely learn to make errors deliberately on clean prompts.
key_findings.evidence: Ablations vary the error fraction and whether erroneous tokens contribute to loss. The paper reports that inference usually follows the correct path directly and that masking wrong tokens is unnecessary for the main gain, suggesting the correction pattern rather than imitation of error dominates in-distribution behavior.

key_findings.claim: Error correction is easier to acquire during pretraining or full continued training than through low-rank fine-tuning.
key_findings.evidence: LoRA across several ranks underperforms direct retry pretraining; full fine-tuning with enough retry tokens works but costs roughly as much as continued pretraining. In contrast, error detection alone is learnable with a small adaptation, separating recognizing an error from changing the generative policy after one.

key_findings.claim: Simple weak-model-generated retry data helps, while more elaborate missed-error constructions add little in the tested setting.
key_findings.evidence: The preparation study compares realistic weak-generator errors with variants that inject or recover missed errors. The conclusion labels weak retry data easy to obtain and beneficial, but the entire evidence base is synthetic grade-school arithmetic, so transfer to noisy human or web corrections is unestablished.

method.core_idea: Make recovery from a wrong reasoning prefix part of next-token pretraining rather than a separate inference-time self-correction loop.
method.mechanism: Generate synthetic math solutions, splice plausible erroneous steps followed by retry markers and corrected steps, pretrain from scratch under controlled token budgets, and ablate masking, error rates, error sources, beam search, LoRA, and full fine-tuning.
assumptions: The synthetic arithmetic generator captures relevant reasoning structure.
Wrong steps are plausible enough to teach recovery rather than trivial marker following.
Token-matched data is a fair compute comparison.
Direct solution accuracy reflects learned correction rather than memorized templates.
Retry-marker conventions transfer to natural correction traces.

techniques.role: Places error and correction in one autoregressive sequence.
Tests whether learning to predict errors is required.
Measures safety and benefit as retries become common.
Tests when correction competence must enter the model.

evaluations.result: Retry-data models outperform token-matched clean-data models across reported settings
Benefits persist and deliberate mistakes remain rare even at high retry rates; masking is unnecessary
evaluations.baseline: Clean data and masked wrong tokens

evaluations.metric: Reasoning accuracy after exposure to retry data
evaluations.result: LoRA falls short; sufficiently large full fine-tuning works at continued-pretraining-like cost
Weak-model retry data helps; more complex missed-error data adds little

limitations: The task distribution is synthetic and much narrower than real mathematical language.
No human-authored correction corpus or frontier-scale model is tested.
The retry marker may create a special mode not present in natural text.
Equal tokens do not necessarily equal generation, filtering, or curriculum cost.
Safety is measured in distribution; malicious or misleading correction traces are not studied.
failure_modes: Low-quality retry data reinforces plausible false corrections.
The model learns marker-conditioned behavior that does not activate after unmarked errors.
Too many erroneous tokens degrade factual priors in broader domains.
Weak generators produce narrow, repetitive error types.
Correction competence fails to transfer outside the synthetic grammar.
A model learns to conceal errors by skipping explicit intermediate steps.
reusable_insights: Distinguish error detection from recovery-policy learning.
Compare correction data at pretraining, continued-training, and parameter-efficient stages.
Measure whether training on errors increases error emission, not only final accuracy.
Use naturally sampled model mistakes before hand-designed corruptions.
Evaluate recovery from unseen error types and unmarked prefixes.
open_questions: Do natural human revisions and verifier-generated traces produce the same gain?
What mixture of clean, error, critique, and correction tokens scales best?
Can models recover when the error occurs in their own hidden reasoning without an explicit marker?
How robust is retry training to incorrect critics and reward hacking?
Does the gain persist on theorem proving, code, science, and open-ended planning?

competitive_landscape.title: Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet
competitive_landscape.difference: Huang et al. show intrinsic multi-round self-correction often fails without external feedback. This paper moves correction examples into pretraining so the one-pass policy learns recovery before deployment.

competitive_landscape.title: STaR: Bootstrapping Reasoning With Reasoning
competitive_landscape.difference: STaR iteratively filters and fine-tunes on successful rationales. Retry pretraining deliberately retains wrong prefixes followed by corrections and tests whether that structure improves a from-scratch model.

competitive_landscape.title: CRITIC: Large Language Models Can Self-Correct with Tool-Interactive Critiquing
competitive_landscape.difference: CRITIC uses tools to critique and revise at inference. The reviewed method aims to internalize recovery through data so ordinary autoregression improves without a runtime loop, but lacks CRITIC's external grounding.

competitive_landscape.title: Let's Verify Step by Step
competitive_landscape.difference: Lightman et al. train process reward models from step labels to select correct reasoning. Retry pretraining changes the generator distribution directly and needs no inference-time verifier, but its supervision is synthetic and much narrower.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: Pretraining on mistakes immediately followed by corrections makes one-pass math reasoning more accurate than equal clean data and teaches a competence that LoRA cannot easily add later.
novelty_assessment.evidence: Controlled synthetic experiments isolate retry structure, safety, masking, error quantity, generation source, search, and training-stage effects.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: Reasoning bootstrapping, process supervision, and inference-time revision are established. The novel contribution is the clean controlled evidence for retaining error-correction trajectories during pretraining. External validity to natural corpora and large models is the decisive missing test.

reviewer_notes: Read all 23 extracted pages, including main synthetic construction, beam/search distinctions, masking and retry-rate sweeps, LoRA/full-training comparison, weak-error generation, conclusion, and extended figures. Four primary arXiv comparators were checked on 2026-08-23.
